'''Jennifer Loros''', also known as '''J.J. Loros''', is a [[Chronobiology|chronobiologist]] leading the field in the study of circadian rhythms in ''[[Neurospora crassa|Neurospora]]''. Her research focuses on circadian oscillators and their control of gene expression in living cells. Currently, Loros is a professor of [[Biochemistry]], [[Cell biology|Cell Biology]], and [[Molecular biology|Molecular]] and [[Systems biology|Systems]] Biology at the [[Geisel School of Medicine|Giesel School of Medicine]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://geiselmed.dartmouth.edu/msb/faculty/|title=Faculty : Department of Molecular and Systems Biology :: Geisel School of Medicine|website=geiselmed.dartmouth.edu|language=en-US|access-date=2017-04-13}}</ref>

== Biography ==

=== Education ===
Loros is from [[Los Altos, California]]. She attended [[Homestead High School (Cupertino, California)|Homestead High School]] and graduated in 1968. Loros then attended both [[Cabrillo College]] and [[Monterey Peninsula College]] and received two associate degrees in [[Biology]] by 1971.<ref name=":2" />

By 1979, Loros received her bachelor's degree in [[Biology]] from [[University of California, Santa Cruz|UC Santa Cruz]]. She went on to complete her PhD in [[Genetics]] from [[Geisel School of Medicine|Dartmouth Medical School]].<ref name=":0" />

=== Career (1988-present) ===
In 1988, Loros began her career in biology at [[Geisel School of Medicine|Dartmouth Medical School]] as a postdoctoral researcher in [[Biochemistry]].<ref name=":2" /> By 1994, Loros earned the position of Research Associate Professor of [[Biochemistry]]<ref name=":2" /> and then accepted the position of associate professor of [[Biochemistry]] in 1996. She then became Professor of [[Biochemistry]] and Professor of [[Genetics]] in 2000 and 2001 respectively.<ref name=":0" />

Loros also leads research at the Dunlap and Loros Laboratories with her husband [[Jay Dunlap]], a fellow chronobiologist and researcher.<ref name=":2" /> Her focus is on the circadian clock in ''[[Neurospora crassa|Neurospora]]'' and its application to the genetic mechanisms of the clock in other organisms.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://geiselmed.dartmouth.edu/dunlaploros/members/current.php|title=Geisel School of Medicine :: Dunlap - Loros Lab :: Lab Members|website=geiselmed.dartmouth.edu|access-date=2017-04-13|archive-date=2017-03-31|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170331074915/http://geiselmed.dartmouth.edu/dunlaploros/members/current.php|url-status=dead}}</ref> Loros, along with [[Jay Dunlap]] and [[Patricia DeCoursey|Patricia J. DeCoursey]], co-authored the text book "Chronobiology: Biological Timekeeping " which was published on June 1, 2004. The text chronicles the field of chronobiology by exploring both past and current discoveries and their relevance to modern society.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://academic.oup.com/icb/article/44/3/266/600929/Chronobiology-Biological-Timekeeping|title=Chronobiology: Biological Timekeeping|last=Giebultowicz|first=Jadwiga|date=2004|journal=Integrative and Comparative Biology|volume=44 |issue=3 |page=266 |doi=10.1093/icb/44.3.266 |pmid=21676707 |access-date=2017-04-30|doi-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Scientific career ==

=== Advancements in methodology  ===
Dr. Loros contributed to advancing research techniques by developing a targeted gene disruption technique for use in [[Neurospora crassa|''Neurospora'']], which had the effect of amplifying gene markers in such a manner as to make identification of low homologous recombination rates possible, which had previously not been the case when using traditional techniques such as [[Southern blot|Southern Blot]] tests.<ref name=":3" /> Gene identification in ''[[Neurospora crassa|Neurospora]]'' was additionally progressed by Loros’ lab when it produced a high density [[Single-nucleotide polymorphism|SNP]] map for ''[[Neurospora crassa|Neurospora]]''.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book|last=Dunlap, J. C., K. A. Borkovich, M. R. Henn, G. E. Turner, M. S. Sachs, N. L. Glass, K. McCluskey, M. Plamann, J. E. Galagan, B. W. Birren, R. L. Weiss, J. P. Townsend, J. J. Loros, M. A. Nelson, R. Lambreghts, H. V. Colot, G. Park, P. Collopy, C. Ringelberg, C. Crew, L. Litvinkova, D. DeCaprio, H. M. Hood, S. Curilla, M. Shi, M. Crawford, M. Koerhsen, P. Montgomery, L. Larson, M. Pearson, T. Kasuga, C. Tian, M. Baştürkmen, L. Altamirano, and J. Xu.|chapter=Enabling a Community to Dissect an Organism: Overview of the Neurospora Functional Genomics Project |date=2007|title=Fungal Genomics |series=Advances in Genetics |volume=57|pages=490–49449–96|doi=10.1016/S0065-2660(06)57002-6 |pmid=17352902 |pmc=3673015 |isbn=9780120176571 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|author1=Dekhang, Rigzin|author2=Cheng Wu|author3=Kristina M. Smith|author4=Teresa M. Lamb|author5=Matthew Peterson|author6=Erin L. Bredeweg|author7=Oneida Ibarra|author8=Jillian M. Emerson|author9=Nirmala Karunarathna|author10=Anna Lyubetskaya|author11=Elham Azizi|author12=Jennifer M. Hurley|author13=Jay C. Dunlap|author14=James E. Galagan|author15=Michael Freitag|author16=Matthew S. Sachs|author17-link=Deborah Bell-Pedersen|author17=Deborah Bell-Pedersen|date=January 2017|title=The Neurospora Transcription Factor ADV-1 Transduces Light Signals and Temporal Information to Control Rhythmic Expression of Genes Involved in Cell Fusion.|journal=Genetics|volume=7 |issue=1 |pages=129–142 |doi=10.1534/g3.116.034298 |pmid=27856696 |pmc=5217103 }}</ref>

Lastly, continuing on with an idea from her post-doc work, Loros resynthesized a gene that codes for [[Luciferase|firefly luciferase]].<ref name=":2" /> Since ''[[Neurospora crassa|Neurospora]]'' has long been a key [[model organism]] in the chronobiology field, modifying this tool has been key in further research. Before this, [[Codon usage bias|codon bias]] prevented effective usage of firefly luciferase in [[Neurospora crassa|''Neurospora'']], problematic as firefly luciferase serves as a reporter to measure transcription in cells. By modifying the firefly luciferase gene, Loros was able to achieve several orders more of light production in ''[[Neurospora crassa|Neurospora]]'', revolutionizing transcription measurements in N. cell cultures. Moreover, her modification to this reporter allowed the &nbsp;[[Frequency (gene)|FRQ]]/WCC feedback loop to be monitored in real time without disturbing the overt rhythms of the system. This in turn provided the tool to distinguish between oscillators not directly in the clock and the circadian clock itself.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Fiedler, M. R., T. Gensheimer, C. Kubisch, and V. Meyer.|date=8 March 2017|title=HisB as Novel Selection Marker for Gene Targeting Approaches in Aspergillus Niger.|journal=BMC Microbiology|volume=17 |issue=1 |page=57 |doi=10.1186/s12866-017-0960-3 |pmid=28274204 |pmc=5343542 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

=== Research into clock-controlled genes and frq  ===
After joining the faculty of the [[Geisel School of Medicine|Giesel School of Medicine]], Loros continued her post-doc research into the regulation of messenger RNA by circadian clocks.<ref name=":4" /> Through sequential rounds of [[Suppression subtractive hybridization|subtractive hybridization]], Loros found 2 such genes that are responsible for transcription in morning specific cultures of ''[[Neurospora crassa|Neurospora]]''. Loros named these two, unlinked, genes ccg-1 and ccg-2, with the initialisms standing for clock-controlled genes, a term which, now prevalent in the circadian clock dialogue, Loros claims to have coined herself.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last=Aronson, B. D., K. A. Johnson, Q. Liu, and J. C. Dunlap.|date=June 1992|title=Molecular Analysis of the Neurospora Clock: Cloning and Characterization of the Frequency and Period-4 Genes.|journal=Chronobiology International|volume=9 |issue=3 |pages=231–239 |doi=10.3109/07420529209064532 |pmid=1535290 }}</ref> Moreover, her work on the [[negative feedback]] loop involved in the FRQ pathway demonstrated that the phosphorylation of negative elements of the clock are not as important in controlling the period as once thought. Loros and her collaborators showed that the nature of the FRQ allele controlled the pace of the clock, not the rate of phosphorylation and degradation of clock elements.

=== Research into photobiology, the White-Collar Complex, and ''Aspergillus fumigatus''  ===
During her post-doc work, Loros remarked upon the possibility of frq being light induced, which was later confirmed by a post-doc fellow.<ref name=":1" /> Turning her attention to the governing body for this light induction, Loros began experimenting with [[White Collar-1|wc-1]] finding that it not only was the mediator for said light induction, but was also necessary for [[Neurospora crassa|''Neurospora''’s]] clock in the absence of light.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Brunner, M., and T. Schafmeier.|date=1 May 2006|title=Transcriptional and Post-transcriptional Regulation of the Circadian Clock of Cyanobacteria and Neurospora.|journal=Genes & Development|volume=20 |issue=9 |pages=1061–1074 |doi=10.1101/gad.1410406 |pmid=16651653 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

[[White Collar-1|Wc-1]], in conjunction with its partner protein, wc-2, was found to be the first described positive element regulator in a circadian feedback loop, with the norm being that of negative regulators. This led to the precedent of the PAS-PAS heterodimers in both animals and fungi alike.<ref name=":1" />

=== The role of metabolism in the circadian system  ===
Recently, Loros has worked on examining the reciprocal relationship between metabolism and circadian rhythm. Using ''[[Neurospora crassa|Neurospora]]'' as her model organism, Loros’ work has revealed how interconnected these two crucial systems are in fungi. These links include both the outputs of each system and how metabolism can directly influence the rhythms set by the clock.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Montenegro-Montero, A., P. Canessa, and L. F. Larrondo.|date=2015|title=Around the Fungal Clock: Recent Advances in the Molecular Study of Circadian Clocks in Neurospora and Other Fungi.|series=Advances in Genetics|volume=92 |pages=107–184 |doi=10.1016/bs.adgen.2015.09.003 |pmid=26639917 |isbn=978-0-12-804014-0 }}</ref>
